title: You’re Still Trying to Make a Dead Parent Finally Be Proud of You.
paragraphs: You’re Still Trying to Make a Dead Parent Finally Be Proud of You.

They may have been gone for years. But somewhere inside you, the child who never heard “I’m proud of you” may still be running, achieving, proving, performing… hoping an absent voice will finally say the words death made impossible.
There is a strange kind of grief nobody warns you about.
It is not simply missing someone who died.
Sometimes it is missing what you never received from them while they were alive.
And those are two very different graves.
Maybe your mother is gone.
Maybe your father is gone.
Maybe everybody remembers them fondly. They tell stories at family gatherings. They post old photographs on birthdays. They say how much they miss them.
And you miss them too.
But buried underneath your grief is something harder to admit.
You are still waiting.
Still waiting for the conversation that never happened.
Still waiting for the apology.
Still waiting for the embrace.
Still waiting for them to notice how hard you tried.
Still waiting to hear...
“I see you.”
“You did well.”
“I’m proud of you.”
“I should have told you that more.”
Maybe you stood beside their coffin and something inside you realized with terrifying finality:
They are never going to say it now.
Yet somehow...
you kept trying to earn it.
That is the wound we need to talk about.
Because your parent may have died...
but the audition didn’t.
You got the promotion.
You bought the house.
You raised the children.
You survived things nobody knows about.
You became responsible.
Dependable.
Successful.
Useful.
Strong.
Maybe you became the person everybody calls when life falls apart.
And somewhere beneath all of that achievement is still a little boy saying, “Dad, look what I did.”
Or a little girl whispering, “Mom, did I finally become someone you could be proud of?”
Nobody hears that voice.
Maybe even you stopped hearing it.
But it may still be directing your life.
That is what makes unresolved approval so powerful.
You can bury a parent without burying your need for their blessing.
You can grieve them and still be angry with them.
You can love them and still acknowledge what they failed to give you.
You can forgive them and still discover wounds that need the healing of Christ.
You can stand at a graveside as an adult while something inside you feels eight years old again.
And perhaps the most painful realization is this:
Some of us are spending our lives trying to win an argument with someone who is no longer here.
“See? I became somebody.”
“See? I wasn’t worthless.”
“See? I proved you wrong.”
“See what I accomplished?”
“Would you love me now?”
And then Scripture walks into that room with a question that sounds almost uncomfortably direct.
Paul writes in Galatians 1:10:
The Greek presses even closer:
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν;”
Arti gar anthrōpous peithō ē ton theon? ē zētō anthrōpois areskein?
In context, Paul is defending the Gospel he received and proclaiming that his allegiance is not governed by human approval. The issue is bigger than insecurity. It is lordship.
Who gets the final vote over who you are?
People?
Or God?
That question becomes devastating when the person whose approval controlled you was your own parent.
Because parental approval is not inherently evil.
A child should be loved.
A child should be encouraged.
A child should hear words that strengthen rather than crush.
A father telling his son, “I’m proud of the man you’re becoming,” can become a memory he carries for decades.
A mother delighting in her daughter can give that girl a sense of safety no trophy can reproduce.
Wanting those things was not weakness.
You were not wrong for wanting to be loved.
The wound began when something good became something ultimate.
When their approval became the courtroom where your worth was continually being tried.
Maybe Dad only noticed excellence.
So you became excellent.
Maybe Mom compared you with your siblings.
So life became a competition.
Maybe affection appeared only when you accomplished something.
So accomplishment became your language for asking to be loved.
Maybe mistakes brought humiliation.
So now failure feels almost unbearable.
Maybe your parent rarely praised you, and whenever you brought home something good, there was always another question.
Why not higher?
Why not first place?
Why not more?
Why can’t you be like them?
And eventually you stopped bringing home report cards.
You started bringing home a life.
Degrees.
Money.
Titles.
Ministry accomplishments.
Children who behave well.
A respectable marriage.
A carefully maintained reputation.
Even spirituality can become part of the performance.
You can serve at church because you love Jesus...
and still secretly need everybody to recognize that you matter.
You can preach Christ while craving applause.
You can give generously while needing somebody to notice.
You can become indispensable because being needed feels dangerously similar to being loved.
That is why Galatians 1:10 cannot remain a decorative Bible verse.
It asks us something.
Whose approval has become your master?
Because Paul ends with an extraordinary expression:
“Χριστοῦ δοῦλος”
Christou doulos.
A servant—a bondservant—of Christ.
That changes everything.
Paul is not saying healthy relationships do not matter.
He is saying human approval cannot occupy Christ’s throne.
And maybe that is where Jesus is meeting you right now.
Not at the polished version of your life.
Not at the awards.
Not at the career.
Not at the ministry statistics.
Not at the bank balance.
Not at the house.
Not at the image everybody else admires.
Jesus is walking toward the child underneath all of it.
The one still holding something up toward an empty chair.
“Look what I did.”
And Christ is not mocking that child.
He is not shaming your longing.
He is exposing the throne that longing quietly built.
Because He loves you too much to let a dead person remain the functional judge of a life Jesus purchased with His own blood.
Read that again.
A dead person does not get to be the final judge of a life Jesus purchased with His blood.
Your father may never tell you what you needed to hear.
Your mother may never come back and explain herself.
There may be no final conversation.
No corrected childhood.
No handwritten letter discovered in a drawer.
No hidden recording.
No miraculous earthly resolution.
Some doors really do close.
Christian hope does not require pretending otherwise.
But the Gospel gives you something infinitely greater than rewriting yesterday.
It gives you a new identity today.
Before Jesus began His public ministry, before the miracles multiplied, before Calvary, the Father declared His pleasure in His beloved Son.
And through faith, our life becomes bound to Christ.
Paul writes elsewhere that those who belong to Jesus receive adoption as God’s children.
That does not mean God becomes a sentimental replacement for whatever our earthly parents failed to be.
It means something much greater.
Your deepest identity is no longer decided by the verdict of human beings.
Not even the human beings whose voices shaped you first.
In Christ, you belong to God.
You do not become valuable because you finally perform well enough.
Grace destroys that transaction.
The Gospel says you could never perform well enough to save yourself.
Neither could I.
Sin is deeper than insecurity.
Our problem is not merely that people failed to approve of us.
Our problem is that we have sinned against a holy God.
We have worshiped created things.
We have built identities around success, approval, control, pleasure, reputation and self.
We have tried to justify ourselves.
And then Jesus Christ stepped into the scandal.
The sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Forgiveness is therefore not a trophy for people who finally became impressive.
It is grace for people who finally stop pretending they can save themselves.
That means you can stop presenting your résumé to the grave.
You can stop whispering your achievements toward someone who cannot answer.
You can stop building monuments out of accomplishments hoping they will somehow travel backward through time and change what your childhood felt like.
Jesus is not asking you to prove that you deserved more love.
He is calling you to Himself.
Maybe your father would have been proud if you earned another million.
Maybe not.
Maybe your mother would finally have approved if you became thinner, richer, more successful, more respected, more religious.
Maybe not.
There was always going to be another finish line.
But Christ does not stand at the next finish line.
Christ stands at the cross.
And the cross destroys our illusion that salvation, identity and righteousness can be achieved.
You come empty-handed.
You repent.
You believe.
You receive grace.
And suddenly the question governing your life begins to change.
Not...
“Would Dad finally be proud?”
Not...
“Would Mom finally approve?”
But...
“Lord Jesus, are You being glorified in me?”
That is freedom.
Not indifference.
Not dishonoring your parents.
Not erasing your memories.
Not pretending the wound never existed.
Freedom is being able to remember them without continuing to perform for them.
Freedom is visiting the grave without bringing your résumé.
Freedom is succeeding without needing success to prove you deserved love.
Freedom is failing without believing failure has erased your worth.
Freedom is forgiving without calling evil good.
Freedom is grieving what you never received without allowing that absence to become your god.
And perhaps forgiveness is part of what Jesus is asking from you.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending your parent did everything right.
It does not require calling neglect loving.
It does not mean abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean boundaries were sinful.
It does not require inventing an apology they never made.
Biblical forgiveness is not historical revisionism.
It is surrendering vengeance and judgment to God.
Sometimes the person who wounded us dies before reconciliation happens.
That leaves a peculiar ache because there is no longer an earthly possibility of hearing, “I was wrong.”
But you do not need their confession before you can begin bringing your wound to Christ.
You can tell Jesus the truth.
“I wanted him to love me.”
“I wanted her to choose me.”
“I wanted them to notice.”
“I wanted just one moment when I didn’t have to earn affection.”
“I am angry.”
“I miss them.”
“I forgive them.”
“I don’t know how to forgive them.”
“Jesus, help me.”
Prayer does not need impressive vocabulary when your heart is bleeding.
Maybe repentance is also necessary.
Because wounded people can turn wounds into idols.
We can spend decades demanding from success what only Christ can give.
We can punish spouses for not supplying the affirmation our parents withheld.
We can pressure children to become evidence that our lives mattered.
We can chase money because money cannot criticize us.
We can become addicted to recognition because applause temporarily silences the old voice.
We can even resent God because He did not give us the parent we thought we needed.
Bring that into the light too.
Jesus already knows.
Grace is not frightened by the truth.
This is what Christ does.
He does not merely decorate our scars.
He redeems sinners.
He confronts what enslaves us, forgives what condemns us, heals what has been wounded, and begins transforming what sin distorted.
This is why our message has always been bigger than inspiration.
From scandal to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal write the final sentence.
Maybe your story began with rejection.
Jesus can still write redemption.
Maybe it began with abandonment.
Jesus can still write belonging.
Maybe your father died before saying the words.
Maybe your mother left you with questions that will remain unanswered on this side of eternity.
Jesus can still write freedom.
Your history matters.
But your history is not your Messiah.
Jesus is.
And if this exposed something you have hidden even from yourself, you do not need to write your entire story publicly.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
Your testimony may become permission for another grieving adult to finally tell the truth.
There may be someone reading the comments tonight who has spent forty years thinking they were the only one.
Do not underestimate what honesty surrendered to Jesus can do.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone on your Facebook friends list may be celebrating promotions, posting family photographs, buying things, working endlessly, smiling publicly...
while privately still trying to impress a parent buried years ago.
Send it privately if tagging them publicly would expose something that is not yours to expose.
Sometimes sharing truth is ministry.
Sometimes one click puts the Gospel in front of a person who would never walk into a church asking for help.
Because old approval wounds do not always surrender in one emotional moment.
You may need these words again when you succeed.
You may need them when you fail.
You may need them on your parent’s birthday.
You may need them on the anniversary of their death.
You may need to remember:
You are no longer required to spend your life auditioning before an empty chair.
It does not.
Not because giving purchases blessing.
It does not.
Not because anyone should pressure you into proving your love for God with money.
Scripture says giving is to come from the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity can genuinely support Gospel work.

Give to your local church and practice Christian generosity according to Scripture, conscience and faithful biblical conviction. If you prayerfully choose to include Gospel Warrior among the ministries you support, receive our gratitude.
It is mission.
It is helping more wounded people encounter Scripture.
Helping another exhausted believer find biblical encouragement at 2:00 in the morning.
Helping another person discover a free Christian book they could not otherwise afford.

Helping us continue writing the uncomfortable articles that do not merely tell people they are wonderful, but lovingly point sinners and sufferers toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, discipleship and Jesus Christ.
Pray for the ministry.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Because this was never supposed to end with Gospel Warrior.
It must end where the Gospel ends...
with Christ.
Maybe tonight you finally need to say something you have been afraid to say.
“Dad, I loved you. But I cannot keep living for your approval.”
“Mom, I miss you. But I cannot keep measuring myself by what you never gave me.”
“I forgive you.”
“I release what I cannot change.”
“And Jesus...
I belong to You.”
You may cry when you say it.
Let yourself cry.
Those tears do not mean you loved your parent too much.
They may mean you are finally admitting how much you wanted to be loved by them.
Then look toward Christ.
The One who knows every secret motive.
Every achievement.
Every failure.
Every childhood memory.
Every funeral.
Every sentence you wish had been spoken.
Every question that followed you home from the cemetery.
He knows.
And He is still calling you away from the exhausting courtroom of human approval and into wholehearted allegiance to Himself.
You cannot go backward and make your childhood different.
You cannot make the dead speak.
You cannot earn yesterday’s missing affirmation tomorrow.
But through Jesus Christ, yesterday does not have to own tomorrow.
So put down the trophy.
Put down the résumé.
Put down the imaginary conversation.
Put down the lifelong audition.
The chair is empty.
But the throne is not.
You spent years hoping an absent parent would finally tell you who you are. The cross is calling you to stop asking the grave for a verdict Jesus Christ has already claimed the right to give.
